    Sub-clustering and per-group pipelines¶

    Python port of the R vignette Sub-clustering and per-group pipelines. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

    Intro¶

    Your first pass of clustering gives you lineages: T cells, B cells, monocytes. What it does not give you is the structure inside those lineages. The highly variable genes and the principal components were chosen to separate a monocyte from a B cell, and on that axis every T cell looks the same. If you crank up the Leiden resolution on the full object you mostly get the lineages chopped into arbitrary pieces, not naive versus memory CD4.

    The fix is to throw the global feature selection away and redo it on the cells you actually care about. That is what SingleCellsSubset is for. It gives you a view onto a subset of a SingleCells object that shares the on-disk counts with the parent, but carries its own empty cache, so HVG, PCA, neighbours and clusters all get recomputed from scratch on the subset alone.

    This vignette assumes you have read the design choices and the PBMC walkthrough. The standard chain is not re-explained here.

    For the annotation we deliberately stay coarse. No CD4 versus CD8 split, no naive versus memory. Lineage only, because the fine structure is exactly what we want the subset to recover.

    Taking a subset¶

    The constructor takes the parent, a column in obs, and the level you want.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    t_cells = bv.SingleCellsSubset(sc, "cell_type", "T cells")

t_cells
    t_cells = bv.SingleCellsSubset(sc, "cell_type", "T cells") t_cells
    Out[7]:
    SingleCellsSubset(
  dir='/var/folders/l0/d50zd8812jg94mhtl8t2swfc0000gn/T/tmpu26qt2s7/pbmc3k',
  group=cell_type = T cells,
  cells=1130, genes=11139,
  hvg=False, pca=False, embeddings=none,
  knn=False, graph=False, magic=False, residuals=False,
  stale=none
)

    The repr tells you the important bit: HVG, PCA, kNN and the graph are all False. Nothing was inherited. The subset reads the parent's stores, so no counts were copied and no files were written, but the ScCache is brand new and the parent's HVG selection was dropped on purpose.

    Everything else behaves like the parent object. The obs table is filtered to the group and held in memory, the var table is untouched, and the usual getters work.

    A note on indices¶

    This is the one place where you can shoot yourself in the foot, so it is worth being explicit. In Python there is a single cell index space: the 0-based position in the parent's stores. cell_idx in the subset's obs, subset_to_original, cells_to_keep and every integer selection you hand to a getter live in it. Integer selections must belong to the subset, and cell ids are matched against the subset's cells only. The one exception is obs(indices=...), which takes row positions within the subset's own obs table.

    cell_indices() maps ids to that space.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    first_three = t_cells.cell_ids()[:3]

# 0-based position in the parent's stores, which is what Rust sees
t_cells.cell_indices(list(first_three))
    first_three = t_cells.cell_ids()[:3] # 0-based position in the parent's stores, which is what Rust sees t_cells.cell_indices(list(first_three))
    Out[10]:
    array([0, 2, 5], dtype=uint32)
    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    assert np.array_equal(
    t_cells.cell_indices(list(first_three)), t_cells.subset_to_original[:3]
)
    assert np.array_equal( t_cells.cell_indices(list(first_three)), t_cells.subset_to_original[:3] )

    The practical upshot: you never translate manually. Hand cell ids or store indices to the getters and let the class deal with it. The cell_idx column is there so you can join results back onto the parent later, which is exactly what we do further down.

    Was any of that worth it? Check how much the feature selection actually moved.

    Copied! 
    global_hvg = sc.map.hvg
subset_hvg = t_cells.map.hvg

len(np.intersect1d(global_hvg, subset_hvg))

    984 of the 2000 genes are shared, so around half of the feature set is different. The subset PCA is built on genes that vary within T cells, which is the whole point.

    Markers for the sub-clusters¶

    Differential expression on the subset is confined to it. Each sub-cluster is tested against the other T sub-clusters, not against every monocyte in the data set.

    Getting the labels back to the parent¶

    So far everything lives in the subset, in memory. To make the labels permanent, or to plot them on the parent's global UMAP, push them into the parent's DuckDB. merge_subset_obs() does the join on cell_idx for you.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    bv.merge_subset_obs(sc, t_cells, cols=["t_subcluster"], prefix_values=True)

sc.obs(filtered=True)["t_subcluster"].value_counts().sort("t_subcluster")
    bv.merge_subset_obs(sc, t_cells, cols=["t_subcluster"], prefix_values=True) sc.obs(filtered=True)["t_subcluster"].value_counts().sort("t_subcluster")
    Merged 1 column(s) for 1130 cells into obs (1570 cells left as NULL).
    Out[17]:
    shape: (3, 2)
    t_subclustercount
    stru32
    null1360
    "T cells_0"587
    "T cells_1"543

    prefix_values=True stamps the subset's group onto every value, so you get T cells_0 rather than a bare 0. Drop it if you want the raw labels. Leave cols out and everything the subset gained that the parent does not have yet gets merged, which after a pipeline run is exactly the new columns.

    The join is a left join, so every cell that was not a T cell gets null. That is the behaviour you want, and the downstream methods respect it.

    Results that already carry their own cell_idx skip the helper entirely. fast_cluster() returns memberships keyed in parent space, so add_obs() takes them directly.

    In [18]:

    Pipelines¶

    Once you are doing this for more than one cell type, writing out HVG, PCA, neighbours and clusters by hand five times gets old. A Pipeline lets you declare the chain once. Steps chain with >>.

    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    subcluster_pipeline = (
    step_hvg(hvg_no=2000)
    >> step_pca(no_pcs=20, sparse_svd=True)
    >> step_neighbours(neighbours_params=NeighboursParams(knn_method="exhaustive"))
    >> step_clusters(res=0.5, name="subcluster")
)

subcluster_pipeline
    subcluster_pipeline = ( step_hvg(hvg_no=2000) >> step_pca(no_pcs=20, sparse_svd=True) >> step_neighbours(neighbours_params=NeighboursParams(knn_method="exhaustive")) >> step_clusters(res=0.5, name="subcluster") ) subcluster_pipeline
    Out[19]:
    Pipeline(n_steps=4, steps=['hvg', 'pca', 'neighbours', 'clusters'])

    If you prefer, Pipeline takes a plain list of steps too.

    In [20]:
    Copied! 
    assert Pipeline(list(subcluster_pipeline.steps)) == subcluster_pipeline
    assert Pipeline(list(subcluster_pipeline.steps)) == subcluster_pipeline

    Pipelines are inert. Nothing runs until you apply one, and the same pipeline works on a SingleCells or a SingleCellsSubset, because each step's function takes either.

    One pipeline, every group¶

    apply_pipeline_per_group() builds the subset for you and returns a dict keyed by group.

    Sizing matters here. PCA with 20 components needs more than 20 cells, so a rare population that the annotation happened to call will fall over and take the whole run with it. Restrict the groups explicitly rather than hoping for the best. On this data set the coarse annotation returned five lineages. The cell below keeps groups with at least 100 cells, a safe margin over what the PCA needs, so the 24 DCs stay out.

    In [22]:
    Copied!

groups_to_run = cell_counts.filter(pl.col("count") >= 100)["cell_type"].to_list()

    Every lineage picked a different feature set, and the shared fraction with the global HVGs is nowhere near complete. Running one global PCA and hoping it resolves everything was never going to work.

    Writing all of that back is one call. merge_subset_obs() takes the values of the dict straight from apply_pipeline_per_group(), checks that no cell shows up twice, and does a single join.

    In [24]:
    Copied!

    sc,
    list(subsets.values()),
    cols=["subcluster"],
    new_names=["fine_label"],
    prefix_values=True,
)

sc.obs(filtered=True)["fine_label"].value_counts().sort("fine_label")
    bv.merge_subset_obs( sc, list(subsets.values()), cols=["subcluster"], new_names=["fine_label"], prefix_values=True, ) sc.obs(filtered=True)["fine_label"].value_counts().sort("fine_label")

    The prefix is doing real work here. Every group's Leiden run starts counting at zero, so without it the T cell 1 and the B cell 1 collapse into one label. Leave it out and you get a warning naming the values that clash. The DCs never went through the pipeline, so they are the null row.

    Source-pure meta cells¶

    All three meta cell generators run on a subset, so you can aggregate per patient and never mix two donors into one meta cell. The catch used to be the last step: you ended up with one MetaCells object per patient and no way to run SCENIC or NMF across the lot. bv.metacells.merge_meta_cells() closes that.

    step_metacells() puts the generation into the chain itself. It is the one step that changes the class of the object, so a pipeline that ends on it hands you MetaCells rather than SingleCellsSubset. Everything before it still runs per patient, which is the point when your samples are split over two plates and need correcting within a donor.

    from bixverse.params import BtMetacellsParams
from bixverse.pipeline import step_harmony, step_metacells

mc_pipeline = (
    step_hvg(hvg_no=2000)
    >> step_pca(no_pcs=20)
    >> step_harmony(batch_column="plate")
    >> step_neighbours(embd_to_use="harmony")
    >> step_metacells(
        "bootstrapped", params=BtMetacellsParams(target_no_metacells=100)
    )
)

per_patient = apply_pipeline_per_group(mc_pipeline, sc, "patient_id")

meta_cells = bv.metacells.merge_meta_cells(per_patient)

    A few things worth knowing:

    • bv.metacells.meta_cells_per_group() does the whole thing in one call if you do not need the per-patient objects. Same arguments, plus method and mc_params.
    • The merged obs table gains a source_id column and the meta cell ids are prefixed with it. original_cell_idx stays in the index space of its own source, so it is only meaningful alongside source_id.
    • Gene spaces are reconciled by "intersect" (the default) or "union", the latter zero-filling genes an input lacks. Both are no-ops when every input came from the same parent object.
    • Counts are carried over untouched. Normalisation is per meta cell, so row-binding leaves it valid.
    • PCA, kNN, sNN and HVG are dropped on merge. They were fitted per patient and mean nothing side by side. Recompute them on the merged object, which is the whole reason for merging.
    • validate_pipeline() checks a chain against a starting class before anything runs. apply_pipeline() and apply_pipeline_per_group() call it for you, so putting step_harmony() after step_metacells() errors immediately instead of after twenty minutes of PCA.

    Caveats and what is next¶

    A few sharp edges to be aware of before you build on this.

    Meta cell memberships come back as positions in the parent's stores, which is what makes them joinable back onto the original object. bv.de.get_pseudobulked() runs on subsets too if aggregation is all you are after.

    Subsets are RNA only, so multi-modal work stays on SingleCellsMultiModal (see the multi-modal vignette).

    Subsets nest conceptually but not in code: you cannot build a SingleCellsSubset from another SingleCellsSubset. If you want a third level, write the labels back to the parent and subset from there.
